title: Minutes Until the Whole Tree Hears
statement:
A binary tree has distinct node values. At minute 0 the node with value start hears a rumor. Every minute, each node that knows the rumor passes it to every node it is directly connected to: its left child, its right child and its parent.

Return the number of minutes until every node has heard it.

examples.why: 4 → 2 (minute 1) → 1 (2) → 3 (3) → 5 and 6 (4). The rumor has to climb up before it can reach the other side.

examples.in: root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, null, 6, null, null, 7], start = 5
examples.why: Below 5 there is only one level, but going up through 2 reaches 6 and 3 at minute 3.

constraints: start is the value of some node
hints: A tree node only knows its children. What would make the spread look like an ordinary graph walk?
Record each node's parent (or build an adjacency list), then BFS from the start node. The number of BFS levels minus one is the answer.

One-pass alternative: for each ancestor of the start node at distance d, the farthest node through its other child is d + height of that other subtree. Take the maximum, together with the start node's own height.

explain.intuition:
The answer is the distance from start to the node farthest away from it. A tree is a graph, the rumor is BFS, and the only obstacle is that nodes have no parent pointers. Add them in one pass (a map from node to parent), then BFS from the start in all three directions and count levels.

You can also do it in one DFS. The farthest node is either below start (its subtree height), or reached by climbing to some ancestor d steps up and then going down into that ancestor's other subtree. So return from each subtree either its height or, if it contains start, the distance to it, and combine.
steps: Walk the tree once and build an adjacency list: each node lists its children and its parent.
BFS from the node whose value is start, with a visited set.
Process the queue one level at a time and count the levels.
Return the level count minus one (minute 0 is the start node).
pitfalls: Only measuring the height below start. The rumor also travels up, as in the second example.
Measuring the tree's height from the root instead of distances from start.
Revisiting the node you came from in the BFS, which loops forever between a parent and a child.

solutions.title: Adjacency list + BFS
solutions.idea: Turn the tree into an undirected graph, then BFS from the start node and count levels.

solutions.title: One DFS: heights and distance to start
solutions.idea: Each subtree reports its height, or its distance to start if start is inside. An ancestor d steps up adds d plus the height of its other subtree as a candidate.

followups: Several nodes start with the rumor at once. What changes in the BFS?
Answer the question for every possible start node in O(n) total. (Hint: the farthest node from anywhere is an end of the tree's diameter.)
lcTitle: Amount of Time for Binary Tree to Be Infected
